newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FEATURE-Traditional medicine booms in Ivory Coast.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Traditional medicine booms in Ivory Coast.

text.p: Long dismissed as primitive, harmful or just plain mumbo-jumbo, traditional medicine is back in fashion in Ivory Coast -- and enjoying new-found respectability.
Individuals, struggling to keep up with the cost of imported pharmaceutical products, are turning more than ever to cheaper, traditional plant-based remedies.

The government, which in the past actively discouraged traditional practices in favour of modern Western-style medicine, is now looking at incorporating some of the better ideas and treatments into the state health system.

"The trouble we have in Africa today is that centuries of colonial rule has changed our mentalities to the extent that we no longer have confidence in ourselves and what we can do for ourselves," says Albert Adou Tano, a traditional doctor.
But perceptions change and Tano and his colleagues, who have formed an association to share ideas, are enjoying the benefits.

"Sometimes, I would go to the drugstore, buy expensive drugs which would not solve my problem but I have stopped that," says Jean-Claude Kouassi, a civil servant and a convert to the benefits of traditional remedies.
DEVALUATION HELPS TRADITIONAL DOCTORS

Orthodox medical services in Ivory Coast were considered expensive even before the CFA franc was devalued by 50 percent in January 1994. Since then, the cost of imported medicines have risen by between 30 and 79 percent -- without corresponding increases in incomes.

Today tradi-practitioners are opening shops in parts of town where they would not previously have been welcome. In November, they joined a range of other local and foreign exhibitors at Abidjan's International Trade Fair.

"Economic factors are forcing the average Ivorian to start taking cost effective decisions in an attempt to satisfy his daily needs," said Tano, who has a consulting room and shop in Abidjan's Plateau business district.
"People from all walks of life come to me for consultations and treatment. Some initially doubted the efficacity of my herbal prescriptions but after use, they always return."

Tano and his colleagues did brisk business at the trade fair, offering what they said were cures to ailments ranging from malaria, cancer, epilepsy, diabetes, rheumatism, sterility -- to poor sexual performance.
His herbal treatment for malaria cost half as much as drugs bought from a pharmacy.
JARS OF CONCOCTIONS IN HERBALIST'S CLINIC
Tano's suburban house in Abidjan serves as pharmaceutical factory, clinic and drugstore. Wooden racks are crammed with large glass jars of herbal concoctions.
"It is from these that I produce all my medicines," Tano says, pointing at dried tropical leaves and roots scattered around the room.
His most famous product is Sarenta, which he says helps improve the condition of AIDS sufferers when combined with Gluitosine, his remedy for prostate ailments.
Ivory Coast's health authorities, keen to cut the nation's imported drug bill, are promoting the use of generic drugs in place of the more expensive brand-name medicines.
Officials say current health policy also targets integration of traditional herbal medicine into the health system -- where they can be shown to be effective.
Not all the claims can be properly tested but health officials have started to monitor some of the more promising treatments.
MOST PEOPLE CAN'T AFFORD WESTERN-STYLE MEDICINE
Government estimates suggest over 90 percent of drugs are imported from France at an annual cost of $80 million.

Officials acknowledge that the cost of health treatment has put Western-style medicine beyond the reach of more than half the nation's 14 million people, most of whom live in the countryside where facilities are lacking.
The government operates various social welfare schemes under which public sector workers pay only 30 percent of treatment costs or receive treatment without paying up front.
It is also taking steps to boost health care in rural areas, as part of economic and social reforms launched by President Henri Konan Bedie under his October 1995 programme.
Tano says tradi-practitioners are ready to play their part.

"We have abundant herbs in this country which we know could be used in curing numerous tropical diseases," he adds, noting that in the past the main obstacle has been "lack of political will and the attitudes of people".
